POLICE FIGHT BACK

By: Nicky Troll | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
48+ criminals taken out by the cops in KZN in the space of three months. Is it excessive or is it the police fighting crime?

Unique Selling Point:
* Topical
* Will divide audiences
* Critical thinking approach to a news lead



Summary:
The KZN police are making headlines with a string of criminals taken out in shoot outs – but are they doing their job or are they crossing a line?

There are arguments for and against. In this piece we explore the level of violent crime and the fight back from police in a province with a brutal bloody history that has seemingly set the scene for status quo. Shoot or be shot.


Further information:
POLICE FIGHTING CRIME
About 48 suspected criminals have been killed by police during shootouts in the province since April, with 17 suspects shot and killed by officers in two weeks at the end of July.

In 2023 there were a spate of drug dealer shootings, also in KZN. The cops in KZN are known for taking out criminals. But it is also a province with a history of bloodshed and brutality.

KZN Police Commissioner Lt. Col. Lucky Mkhwanazi says the police is at war and he is defending what some experts are questioning.

"We are dealing with serious criminals here. Not just criminals who steal, but criminals who kill. We are at war. When you take war to the criminals as the police, the experts must give us space. This is a battleground and we are fighting; we are not negotiating," Mkhwanazi warned.

Mkhwanazi is also not the top brass that leads from an office building away from the frontlines, he has been known to go down to crime scenes, to protests and to directly get involved to diffuse tense situations.

He doesn’t shy away from the issues either. In 2022, Mkhwanazi called for the sale of alcohol to be banned in townships and rural areas. The sentiment came after 21 people were killed in separate tavern shootings in the province. During the infamous July unrest in 2021, Mkhwanazi spoke out against politicians who wanted to interfere with police operations. Now he’s questioning the experience of the experts calling out the recent surge of criminal shootings.

Some security experts are calling these shooting police success stories – they’ve said, we should be asking why there aren’t more successful operations in other provinces? Could it be that the KZN cops are working intelligence and getting results – because at the end of the day the suspects are often armed and willing to put up a fight to avoid arrest.

POLICE CROSSING A LINE
The head of Justice and Violence Prevention at the Institute for Security Studies, Gareth Newham, said police operations were taking place mostly at night or the early hours of the morning - which raised eyebrows.

"In this case, we depend only on the police's word. Often, most or all the suspects are killed, so we are not getting another [version of what happened]. When you see this shift in police shootouts, you need to have some independent inquiry to look at what happened in every incident," Newham.

"This has also increased from 104 [suspected criminals killed] in 2019/20 to 142 in 2022/23.
"Given the high levels of police corruption and low levels of public trust, it is important that when we see an escalation of violence between the police and suspects, there is an independent inquiry into what is happening. In some of these killings, innocent people have been killed," he said. Newham added that the killing of innocent people was one of a number of reasons why the police should plan their operations to avoid bloodshed. "Questions have to be asked about whether or to what extent these killings or violent engagements between criminal suspects and police can be avoided.
Pierre de Vos – South African Constitutional Law Expert has also pointed out some red flags. The paid out R2 billion in the past four years in wrongful arrest cases. He pointed out that the police also had to pay out hundreds of millions of rands for people that they had wrongfully assaulted, shot, or to the families of people they have killed.

Legally speaking he cautions against the parameters of police duties: “What is clear is that police job is not to take the law into their own hands and to decide who is guilty or not, and then, to kill them if there's an opportunity to do so. That is. That would be murder. It it is, very dangerous because, today the police actually identify a real dangerous criminal tomorrow they identify you or me, and they come and shoot us. So while some of these shootouts might actually really be justified, the police's job is to try and arrest people and to do so without killing them or shooting them, and then to bring them to the court where they can actually be tried and convicted, so that we know that the people who are being punished are actually the ones who are guilty of a threat.”

TREATMENT
This story should have a newsy scene setter, incorporating a number of news clips to set the tone of violent crime in KZN, and then to highlight the number of shootings. Interviews to be filmed with two cameras on the subject. Some graphics to detail stats, and then some CCTV footage of CIT robberies, kidnappings, ATM bombings and hits to bring in the reality of violent crime.



INTERVIEWS
- LT COL LUCKY MKHWANAZI – KZN Police Commissioner (KZN)
** We’ve got an in and it looks very positive that we’ll get him for a one on one – but I didn’t want to formally confirm it yet before your sign off.
- GARETH NEWHAM – Institute for Security Studies (PTA)
- CRIMINOLOGIST – Speaking to the current fabric of society – the rise of violent crime and the dangerous game of balancing the desperation for a fight back and the need to ensure criminal justice processes run its course.
- HIDDEN ID COP – a policeman currently in SAPS working on this level of operations that has come face to face with the violent criminals and has had colleagues shot and killed in these shootouts.

** The point of having a second police voice is that while Mkhwanazi will be outspoken, the frontline cop will paint a picture of the day to day reality.

* Archive footage of Mkhwanazi addressing media – might be able to get away with news clips under fair use
* Location for hidden ID interview

STRUCTURE: POLICE FIGHT BACK

VISUALS – CRIME RE-ENACTMENTS // CCTV CRIME

VO: As our country's crime rate soars…

UPSOUND – NEWS REPORTS CRIME STATS

VO: …police in KwaZulu Natal are taking the fight to the criminals.

VISUALS - COPS RUNNING / CHASING

LINK: KZN is a volatile province with a history of violent crime, contract killings, assassinations and taxi wars. In the middle of this. The police are developing a notorious reputation. Because more and more suspects are being gunned down in deadly shootouts.

UPSOUND - NEWS REPORTS… Shootings audio over each other…

VO: The body count keeps climbing – around 100 criminals have been fatally shot, by police in KZN, since the start of 2024.

AUDIO / VISUAL MOMENT – GUN SHOTS

VO: Part of former Police Minister Bheki Cele's controversial legacy

UPSOUND - Shoot to kill

VO: … or the approach of a Provincial Commissioner fed up with violent crime?

MKHWANAZI: We are taking a war to the criminal, this is a battleground, we are fighting we are not negotiating.
CREDIT - KwaZulu-Natal Provincial Government

GOVAN: it seems like you're encouraging the police to shoot.
MKHWANAZI: // I'm encouraging the police not to die with their weapons in their hands.

VO: Whatever the motivation, does the spike in criminal deaths show a dangerous sub-culture taking root within the police?

Gareth Newham heads up Justice and Violence Prevention at the Institute for Security Studies.

GARETH: // it is kind of a badge of honour the more shootings you've been in, // in police units that are often dealing with high risk situations.

VO: This man is a member of one of those police units.

INTRO CLIP – COP we deal with the worst of the worst.

VO: We’ve hidden his identity because he’s breaking rank by speaking to us.

GOVAN: Are you proud of what you do, the fact that you're involved in all these shootings?
COP: Not proud to be involved in shootings, but proud to be a policeman.

VO: Increasingly, questions are being asked of the man in charge. Is the commissioner a strategist deploying resources effectively, or a hardcore crusader?

GARETH: // he distinguished himself in by pushing back on unlawful, inappropriate political interference. // somebody who takes his job incredibly seriously has quite high standards of himself and others. //

VO: As a member of the police top brass, Lt. Gen. Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi cuts against the grain.

GOVAN: You project fearlessness when you're walking the streets. Why do you make it your job to be out in the environment so much?
MKHWANAZI: My position puts me here in the in the boardroom that most, most of the time // But, I believe to strategize less and execute more // we plan once, but we must be out there and execute more //

VO: In 1993, he started out in public order policing, eventually heading up South Africa’s most elite police unit – the Special Task Force.

Now Mkhwanazi is shaking up policing in KZN - after the 2021 looting and flood disasters, the province is prioritizing proactive policing - ensuring its officers get the latest training and setting up smaller, specialized units that aren’t locally based.

He’s often seen at crime scenes and operations, like this recent face-off with taxi bosses.

UPSOUND – TALKING TO TAXI BOSSES?
SABC TAXI FIGHT BACK 5.24 - You cannot break the law then when the police do their work, you fight them. When you decide to fight police, let it be clear that you are starting war. //end on impi.

GOVAN: When the police commissioner says we're at war with criminals, what do you think of that.
GARETH: // police officers, in democracies that are professional police, are not at war with anybody // as soon as you start talking in a military style term, a war, it suggests that we're going to go out to search and destroy, You go to kill the enemy. // the police are not generally at war, the police should generally see themselves as providing a service.

VO: But those on the frontlines, say facing ruthless repeat offenders can often feel like a war.

COP: Come work with us. One day. Let's see if you will have the same attitude when you are facing a rattling noise of a AK 47 assault rifle
GOVAN: Sjoh!
COP: Then let's see if you're going to say the police are heavy handed

VO: And there’s no shortage of illegal weapons on our streets. With at least 2-million illicit guns circulating in the country, facing off with criminals often results in gun battles.

COP: We do not go out every morning and saying no, we are going to kill suspects. But that's the motto of these suspects. They are going to go do this robbery, and anybody who comes in their way is collateral damage. We do not think that way.
GOVAN: People think you're a law unto yourselves.
COP: We make a decision on a split second. We don't have the time to think, okay, let's wait for him to drop his gun down. // It's either them or us.

AUDIO BREAK – BREATHER

VO: On average 400 criminals are killed by police every year. Since January, ten KZN police officers have been killed in the line of duty .

Fighting crime is a high risk job - 39 police officers were honoured at a somber commemoration earlier this month.

MKHWANAZI: People are dying, both police, law enforcement and criminals and perhaps innocent people as well, because there's quite a lot of them that are dying. // that were killed by the criminals. // The number is is three times that. // the life of the of the criminals should not be worshipped, it should not be protected. // an innocent person is the one that // we must care about more than we care about the criminal.

LINK: The police are meant to protect people and arrest suspects. But how much force is acceptable when dealing with armed, hardened criminals?

VO: KZN isn’t the most dangerous province when it comes to violent crime – it ranks third, but it accounts for the majority of criminals shot and killed by police .

Sam Sole is from the Amabhungane Centre For Investigative Journalism.

SAM: when you're operating, // at the boundaries of the, of the law, and you're relying on the fact that you have political or public support, those winds can change
GOVAN // IIs the increase in shootings undermining the fight against organized crime?
SAM: A lot of the kind of crime networks, you know, one soldier can be replaced by, by another. And unless we kind of come to grips with, the people who are higher up the food chain // we're not going to make a particularly large dent.

VO: Critics say a dangerous culture is emerging in KZN policing where, rather than a service, the SAPS is seen as a force that’s become investigator, judge and executioner.

GOVAN: Isn't it better to arrest?
MKHWANAZI: We always arrest. That's why the numbers speaks for themselves.
GOVAN: Well, lots of criminals are dying. That can't be arrested.
MKHWANAZI: // If one out of ten dies. Is that a lot? // we are doing more arrest than shooting. The unfortunate part is that the media perhaps doesn't cover much of the arrest we effect, but they cover more on the on the shooting.

UPSOUND // news clip blocks – xx shot, xx shot…

SAM: These killings, lawful or not, are being given positive publicity.
GOVAN: Why you think there is massive public support for essentially killing criminals?
SAM: // We have a, a crime crisis, people feel helpless. People feel nothing is being done. But, you know, it's really an indictment, in my view, of, the Detective Service and the prosecution service.

NOTE ON CONVICTION RATES

VO: Failures in the criminal justice system, mean that police are arresting repeat offenders again and again. When comparing the number of serious and violent crime cases investigated to successful prosecutions in court, South Africa’s conviction rates are amongst the lowest in the world.

MKHWANAZI: // in our country, we talk about life sentence in prison that you are given. It's actually not life. You don't stay there until you die. You stay there for two years, and you’re back.
GOVAN: Commissioner, are you not concerned that the police will become trigger happy?
MKHWANAZI: I'm concerned about the psychological effect that has the police officers. // There's no joy of a police officer shooting and killing someone. // The community out there do celebrate but the police, don't. //we don’t because we are left with police officers that traumatized psychologically.

NOTES ON POLICE TRAUMA

VO: Police officers operate under constant physical, emotional and psychological stress often resulting in anxiety and trauma, which can lead to burnout and in extreme scenarios even suicide .

With decades of experience, gunfights still rattle police officers.

COP: we need to adjust and go home and become a dad, become a husband, become a boyfriend, become a father
GOVAN: after JUST, killing someone.
COP: After just killing someone. Personally, when I go home, I just sit outside for ten minutes, take out my shoes and just take a deep breath. //And then you have to walk into the house, shower and then pretend, and put that aside until the next call.
GOVAN: It seems impossible.
COP: // it's like an out of, out-of-body experience. //It's never easy taking someone's life. // But, if you look at the bigger picture, we prevented more crimes from happening.

AUDIO BREATH

SAM: what's important is for the detective service to be capacitated for, the police to rebuild, a proper intelligence service, // to do the normal things that, police work requires and to do them better and more effectively. Unless we fix the NPA //there's going to be the siren call for, //strongmen, // seen popularly as people who can bring order
GOVAN: Like MKHWANAZI?
SAM: like MKHWANAZI

VO: It’s a policing style emerging in other provinces. In Gauteng, several suspects were recently also shot and killed by the police. Provincial Commissioner, Lt Gen Tommy Mthombeni echoed his KZN counterpart’s tough stance.

UPSOUND: NEWZROOM CLIP - As we know some of them they are daring, we are up for them and we will meet them on the streets.”

AUDIO BREATH

GARETH: // Police officers do know that if they break the law, doesn't matter what the commander said // they get investigated. They're the ones in the dock, not the commander.

VO: If a shooting is deemed unlawful, officers can be charged with murder. This officer has been down that road, but was eventually cleared after a lengthy investigation and court case.

GOVAN: Do you worry that you could be in the dock again?
COP: All the time. All the time. But, if we hesitate, we are going to die // I would rather be charged for murder than having my family mourn for me in a coffin.


GOVAN: Is it a case of shoot or be shot?
MKHWANAZI: If that criminal starts the fight, then the only, the only thing we can do in return is to give him the fight.But it's not. Our intention is to give a fight.

BREATHER - GUNSHOTS FIRED – visual and audio…


PROMOS

PROMO 1

VO: Nearly 100 Criminals – shot and killed - in KZN - by cops.

MKHWANAZI: If that criminal starts the fight, then the only, the only thing we can do in return is to give him the fight

VO: But are police officers becoming a law unto themselves or are they just refusing to back down.

SAM: //whatever the justification // dead men tell no tales.



PROMO 2
UPSOUND: NEWS REPORTS xx shot, xx shot, xx shot

VO: Criminal bodies are piling up in KZN.

SAM: when you're operating, // at the boundaries of the, of the law, and you're relying on the fact that you have political or public support, those winds can change

VO: Is this the work of trigger happy cops or the culmination of a long overdue fight back to spiralling violent crime trends?

COP: We deal with the worst of the worst // It’s either us or them.


PROMO 3
VO: Gunfights between cops and criminals are going down almost every week in KZN.

COP: // it's like an out of, out-of-body experience. // if we hesitate, we are going to die

VO: The bodies of criminals are piling up with close to 100 since January.

And the cops are not backing down.

MKHWANAZI: // I'm encouraging the police not to die with their weapons in their hands.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): 48+ criminals taken out by the cops in KZN in the space of three months. Is it excessive or is it the police fighting crime?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: * Topical * Will divide audiences * Critical thinking approach to a news lead
metadata.Summary: The KZN police are making headlines with a string of criminals taken out in shoot outs – but are they doing their job or are they crossing a line? There are arguments for and against. In this piece we explore the level of violent crime and the fight back from police in a province with a brutal bloody history that has seemingly set the scene for status quo. Shoot or be shot.
metadata.Further information: POLICE FIGHTING CRIME About 48 suspected criminals have been killed by police during shootouts in the province since April, with 17 suspects shot and killed by officers in two weeks at the end of July. In 2023 there were a spate of drug dealer shootings, also in KZN. The cops in KZN are known for taking out criminals. But it is also a province with a history of bloodshed and brutality. KZN Police Commissioner Lt. Col. Lucky Mkhwanazi says the police is at war and he is defending what some experts are questioning. "We are dealing with serious criminals here. Not just criminals who steal, but criminals who kill. We are at war. When you take war to the criminals as the police, the experts must give us space. This is a battleground and we are fighting; we are not negotiating," Mkhwanazi warned. Mkhwanazi is also not the top brass that leads from an office building away from the frontlines, he has been known to go down to crime scenes, to protests and to directly get involved to diffuse tense situations. He doesn’t shy away from the issues either. In 2022, Mkhwanazi called for the sale of alcohol to be banned in townships and rural areas. The sentiment came after 21 people were killed in separate tavern shootings in the province. During the infamous July unrest in 2021, Mkhwanazi spoke out against politicians who wanted to interfere with police operations. Now he’s questioning the experience of the experts calling out the recent surge of criminal shootings. Some security experts are calling these shooting police success stories – they’ve said, we should be asking why there aren’t more successful operations in other provinces? Could it be that the KZN cops are working intelligence and getting results – because at the end of the day the suspects are often armed and willing to put up a fight to avoid arrest. POLICE CROSSING A LINE The head of Justice and Violence Prevention at the Institute for Security Studies, Gareth Newham, said police operations were taking place mostly at night or the early hours of the morning - which raised eyebrows. "In this case, we depend only on the police's word. Often, most or all the suspects are killed, so we are not getting another [version of what happened]. When you see this shift in police shootouts, you need to have some independent inquiry to look at what happened in every incident," Newham. "This has also increased from 104 [suspected criminals killed] in 2019/20 to 142 in 2022/23. "Given the high levels of police corruption and low levels of public trust, it is important that when we see an escalation of violence between the police and suspects, there is an independent inquiry into what is happening. In some of these killings, innocent people have been killed," he said. Newham added that the killing of innocent people was one of a number of reasons why the police should plan their operations to avoid bloodshed. "Questions have to be asked about whether or to what extent these killings or violent engagements between criminal suspects and police can be avoided. Pierre de Vos – South African Constitutional Law Expert has also pointed out some red flags. The paid out R2 billion in the past four years in wrongful arrest cases. He pointed out that the police also had to pay out hundreds of millions of rands for people that they had wrongfully assaulted, shot, or to the families of people they have killed. Legally speaking he cautions against the parameters of police duties: “What is clear is that police job is not to take the law into their own hands and to decide who is guilty or not, and then, to kill them if there's an opportunity to do so. That is. That would be murder. It it is, very dangerous because, today the police actually identify a real dangerous criminal tomorrow they identify you or me, and they come and shoot us. So while some of these shootouts might actually really be justified, the police's job is to try and arrest people and to do so without killing them or shooting them, and then to bring them to the court where they can actually be tried and convicted, so that we know that the people who are being punished are actually the ones who are guilty of a threat.” TREATMENT This story should have a newsy scene setter, incorporating a number of news clips to set the tone of violent crime in KZN, and then to highlight the number of shootings. Interviews to be filmed with two cameras on the subject. Some graphics to detail stats, and then some CCTV footage of CIT robberies, kidnappings, ATM bombings and hits to bring in the reality of violent crime. INTERVIEWS - LT COL LUCKY MKHWANAZI – KZN Police Commissioner (KZN) ** We’ve got an in and it looks very positive that we’ll get him for a one on one – but I didn’t want to formally confirm it yet before your sign off. - GARETH NEWHAM – Institute for Security Studies (PTA) - CRIMINOLOGIST – Speaking to the current fabric of society – the rise of violent crime and the dangerous game of balancing the desperation for a fight back and the need to ensure criminal justice processes run its course. - HIDDEN ID COP – a policeman currently in SAPS working on this level of operations that has come face to face with the violent criminals and has had colleagues shot and killed in these shootouts. ** The point of having a second police voice is that while Mkhwanazi will be outspoken, the frontline cop will paint a picture of the day to day reality.
